summary: This informational memo describes how an email client should handle voice and fax messages, including those sent using the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM). It gives guidance on what a receiving client should expect and do with such messages.

plainLanguage.summary: Email can carry voice messages and faxes, not just text, and a mail program that treats them as ordinary text fails in small annoying ways. RFC 4024 gives client designers a list of behaviours: show a phone icon, show the length in seconds, open an audio player, and only mark the message read once the audio has actually played.

questions: how should email clients handle voice messages
voice profile for internet mail client behaviour
how should voice messages appear in email
when should a voice message be marked as read
how should clients display message duration
subtitle: How an email client should show and handle voice and fax mail, from the icon to the read flag.

tldr.problem: Email clients are built for text, so a voice or fax message that arrives by mail shows a kilobyte size, opens in a text editor, and can be marked read before anyone has listened to or viewed it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC tells clients to read the Message-Context header to learn the primary content type, then pick the icon, the size unit, the viewer and the moment of marking-as-read to match that type.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document: guidance for client implementers, with no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Voice and Fax in the Mailbox
sections.content:
RFC 4024 describes how a messaging client should behave when it receives voice or fax messages, including messages sent with the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM). It is an Informational document: it guides implementers and does not define a wire protocol.

As messaging grows into unified messaging, a single mailbox can hold text, voice and fax parts. Each media type has its own habits: users open text in an editor, voice in an audio player and fax in an image viewer, and they measure size in kilobytes, seconds and pages. A message with more than one type is a mixed media message.

The RFC hangs its guidance on the Message-Context header field, which says whether the message is voice mail, fax or text. The client reads that header to choose its behaviour. The document aims at all client forms, from graphical programs on computers to small screens and telephone user interfaces (TUI) that read mail aloud, because the user's expectation of behaviour does not change with the interface.
sections.plainLanguage: One mailbox can now hold text, voice and fax. This document tells a mail program how to tell them apart, using a header that names the main content type, and how to treat each type the way a user expects.

sections.title: Icons, Earcons and the Sender's Number
sections.content:
The client should show a cue that says what kind of message this is. On a graphical interface the RFC suggests a telephone icon for voice, a fax machine for fax and an envelope for text. A telephone interface should use a short spoken prompt, called an earcon, such as "voice message".

The cue should reflect the primary content from the Message-Context header, and it can also show read state: a telephone with the receiver off-hook for a played voice message, a fax machine with paper at the bottom for a viewed fax, an open envelope for a read text message. The RFC notes that some clients instead bold unread rows in the list.

Message lists also normally show a sender column. For a voice or fax message the origin is a telephone or fax number, which the user needs in order to call back. The RFC says the client should display that number accurately and separately, not squeeze it into an email address. A dedicated header field carries the digits; the client adds any separating characters itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Show a phone, a fax machine or an envelope so the user can see the message type at a glance, and change the picture once the message has been played or viewed. Show the caller's real telephone number in the list so the user can call back.

sections.title: Showing Message Size in Useful Units
sections.content:
Kilobytes suit text but say little about voice or fax. A user deciding whether to listen now wants the duration in seconds; for a fax, the number of pages. The size the client shows should describe the primary content type from Message-Context.

The RFC offers three ways to carry this information and favours the first. The preferred route uses the Content-Duration MIME header from RFC 3803 on the main audio body part; a client may add up the lengths of several audio parts. For fax a new header along the same lines, Content-Page-Length, could carry the page count, for example Content-Page-Length:3.

The second route puts a length parameter on the Content-Type header at the source, for example Content-Type:audio/*; length=50 or Content-Type:image/tiff; pages=3. The third puts the length in the Subject line, for example Subject=Voice Message (0:04), which needs no client changes but overloads the subject field.
sections.plainLanguage: Count voice in seconds and fax in pages, not in kilobytes. The RFC prefers a dedicated length header, but also describes passing the length in the Content-Type header or in the subject line.

sections.title: Opening the Right Media Viewer
sections.content:
When the user opens a message, the client should open the viewer that suits the primary content: an audio player for voice, an image viewer for fax, a text editor for text. On a telephone interface the same content is rendered as sound. The Message-Context header tells the client which viewer to use; when several body parts exist, the viewer follows the part the user selected.

When more than one viewer can handle a media type, the client should ask the user to pick on the first occasion, then use that choice as the default for that type. The user must be able to change the default later.

The viewer need not live inside the client. The RFC's examples: a user plays a voice message from a graphical client but the audio comes out over a telephone because the desktop has no speakers, and a user listening to the inbox by telephone prints a fax to a nearby machine instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a voice message should start an audio player, a fax should open an image viewer, and text should open an editor. If several viewers fit, ask once, remember the answer, and let the user change it. The player or printer can even sit on a different device.

sections.title: Marking a Message as Read
sections.content:
Users need to see which messages are still unread. The common default marks a message read as soon as its first body part, usually the text part, is viewed. For voice and fax messages the RFC says that default is wrong: a voice message is read only once the audio has been played, and a fax only once the image has been viewed.

For an IMAP4 client this means delaying the \SEEN flag. In the RFC's procedure, the flag is set only after the first attachment of the primary content type has been opened. If Message-Context says voice message, \SEEN is set after the primary voice part, identified by content-disposition or content-criticality, is opened.

This feature is mostly a local matter of client implementation; no new protocol machinery is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not mark a voice message read until the audio has played, or a fax until the image has been seen. In IMAP terms, set the seen flag only after the main content part is opened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that following its guidance improves the user experience but does not make a client safe. A client only interprets the messages it receives and is not responsible for their format. A message can therefore be spoofed or masquerade as something it is not, and the RFC's example is a message dressed up as a voice message, complete with the voice icon, that is not one, in order to fool the end user into a desired behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: The icon and the size come from the message itself, so a forged message can lie about its type. These behaviours improve handling, not safety.

viz.caption: FIVE CLIENT BEHAVIOURS FOR VOICE AND FAX MAIL (RFC 4024)

items.title: Icon
items.text: Telephone, fax machine or envelope, from Message-Context.

items.title: Sender number
items.text: Show the origin's telephone number in its own column.

items.title: Size
items.text: Voice in seconds, fax in pages, not kilobytes.

items.title: Viewer
items.text: Audio player, image viewer or text editor for the main part.

items.title: Read state
items.text: Mark read only after the main content is played or viewed.
